Ninety days is long enough to change how a finance team works and short
enough that one person can hold the whole thing in their head. What
follows is a plan for that period, then a curriculum you can teach
yourself, in your own meeting room, with no outside help and no budget
beyond people's time.

The plan assumes a finance function of somewhere between five and fifty
people. Smaller than that and you compress the phases; larger and you run
this in one department first and treat the rest of the organisation as a
later problem. It also assumes you already have access to some tool — a
general-purpose assistant, an enterprise-tier version of one, or an AI
feature inside software you already pay for. Choosing the tool is a
separate exercise. This section is about what happens after the licence
exists.

Two warnings before you start. First, none of the numbers in this section
are benchmarks, because there are none worth quoting; the only numbers
that will matter to you are the ones your own team records. Second, this
is general guidance on running a change in a team. Anything touching
confidentiality, client consent, professional standards, data protection
or your engagement terms differs by jurisdiction and changes over time.
Check your own position with your professional body, your regulator and
whoever handles your data obligations before you commit to anything here.

## Part one: the ninety-day plan

### What you settle before day one

Four decisions, made once, in writing. They take an hour. Skipping them is
what causes most of the mess later.

**Who owns this.** One named person, not a committee. They do not have to
be the most senior person in the room and they should not be your busiest
month-end resource. They need enough standing to say "not yet" to a
partner.

**What you will measure.** Two things only: the time a task takes end to
end, and whether the output needed rework. Not how many people logged in.
Not how many prompts were run. Enthusiasm is not a measure; it is a mood,
and it evaporates around the twentieth of the month.

**The one rule that applies from day one**, before any policy is written:
nothing produced with an assistant leaves the team — not to a client, not
to a board, not to a regulator, not to a colleague outside finance —
without a named human who has checked it and is willing to have their name
on it. That sentence can go in an email this afternoon. The full policy
comes later.

**What is not going in.** Decide, now, what data does not get pasted into
anything until the policy exists. As a starting position: client-
identifiable information, personal data, anything under an NDA, anything
price-sensitive, anything you would not send to an external printer.
Whether that starting position is right for you depends on your tool's
terms, your contracts and your local rules. Read the terms; do not assume.

| Role | Who it usually is | What they own | Realistic time cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sponsor | FD, controller, managing partner | Says yes to the pilot, protects the time, hears the results | 1 hour a month |
| Owner | A manager with credibility | The plan, the log, the policy draft, the sessions | Half a day a week for 90 days |
| Pilot group | 3–5 people across levels | Doing the two use cases and recording honestly | 2–3 hours a week |
| Reviewer | A senior who is already the quality backstop | Signing off pilot output, flagging what they had to fix | Their normal review time |
| Data/IT contact | Whoever handles systems and contracts | Tool terms, access, what data may go where | 2 hours in month one |

### Phase one — Days 1 to 30: contain it, then choose

**The goal.** Two things by day 30: a written policy people have actually
read, and two chosen use cases with a baseline measurement. Nothing else.
You are not trying to produce results this month. You are trying to stop
the uncontrolled version of this happening while you think.

**Week 1 — find out what is already happening.**
The owner asks every person in the team, individually and without
consequence, what they have already used and what for. Do this in person
or in a short call, not in a form. Say plainly that nobody is in trouble
and that you need the truth to write a sensible policy. You will usually
find more than you expected, including someone who has been pasting things
they should not have. React to that with a fix, not a disciplinary — this
week is the only chance you get to hear the truth cheaply.

*Who:* owner. *Done when:* you have a written list of current use, tool by
tool, person by person, and you have told the whole team the one rule
above.

**Week 2 — draft the policy.**
Short. Two pages at most, because nobody reads four. It needs to cover:
which tools are approved and which are not; what data may never be entered
and what may; that a named human reviews everything before it leaves; how
you record that a review happened; what to do when someone thinks the tool
got something wrong; and who to ask when the policy does not cover the
situation. Have your data/IT contact check it against your tool's terms
and your obligations. If you have client confidentiality duties, get the
consent question answered properly rather than assumed — that answer
differs by jurisdiction and by engagement letter.

*Who:* owner drafts, sponsor approves, data/IT contact checks.
*Done when:* the policy exists, the sponsor has signed it, and it has been
sent to everyone with a request to reply "read".

**Week 3 — choose two use cases.**
Two. Not ten. The temptation is to list every candidate and start them
all, which produces ten half-finished experiments and no evidence about
any of them. Pick using four tests: the task happens at least monthly; it
currently eats time you can name; a wrong answer is caught by someone
before it does damage; and you can tell within a week whether the output
was good. Good early candidates tend to be drafting and summarising work
with a strong review step already around them. Poor early candidates are
anything where an error goes straight out of the door.

*Who:* owner and pilot group, sponsor decides ties. *Done when:* two use
cases are written down in one sentence each, with the name of the person
who reviews the output.

**Week 4 — measure the "before".**
For each of the two use cases, record how long it takes now and how much
rework it currently needs, using the log in the table below. Be honest
that this baseline is an estimate — people are poor at recalling how long
things took, and the act of measuring changes the number. Record it
anyway, and label it as an estimate wherever you quote it later. A soft
baseline you admit is soft beats a precise-sounding figure you invented.

| Date | Task | Who | Minutes, unassisted (est.) | Minutes, assisted | Review minutes | Rework needed? | What went wrong |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

*Who:* pilot group. *Done when:* at least three baseline observations per
use case exist, and everyone in the pilot group has run Level 1 of the
curriculum.

**How phase one most commonly fails.** Someone senior sees a demonstration,
gets interested, and the scope grows in a fortnight from two use cases to
"a strategy". You end up with a slide deck, no baseline and no policy,
while the team quietly carries on doing whatever it was already doing. The
defence is the written pair of use cases: everything else goes on a list
marked "after day 90", and the list is shown, not argued with.

The second failure is a policy written to be safe rather than to be
followed — a document that bans everything, which people comply with by
not telling you what they do. If your policy would make the honest answers
you got in week 1 into sackable offences, you have written the wrong
policy.

### Phase two — Days 31 to 60: run a real pilot

**The goal.** Evidence. By day 60 you want thirty or so logged
observations across your two use cases and a clear, unexcited sense of
whether either one is better, worse or the same.

**Week 5 — train and start.**
Pilot group completes Levels 1 and 2 of the curriculum. They begin using
the assistant on the two chosen use cases only. They log every single run,
including the ones they abandoned halfway. Abandoned runs are data;
quietly dropping them is how a pilot lies to you.

*Who:* owner trains, pilot group runs. *Done when:* every pilot member has
logged at least two runs.

**Week 6 — first honest look.**
Thirty minutes with the pilot group. Not a status update — a specific
question to each person: "Show me the worst output you got this week."
Then: "What did you have to fix?" The reviewer reports what they corrected
before sign-off. Write down the failure types. You are building a list of
what this tool gets wrong on your work specifically, which is more useful
than any general warning anyone can give you.

*Who:* owner chairs, reviewer contributes. *Done when:* a written list of
observed failure types exists and has been circulated to the pilot group.

**Week 7 — tighten, do not widen.**
Take what you learned in week 6 and improve the prompts, not the scope.
This is the week the pilot group does Level 3. If a use case is clearly
not working, say so out loud now and either fix the prompt once or drop
it. Dropping one of two use cases at week 7 is a normal outcome, not a
defeat, and it is much cheaper than dropping it at week 12.

*Who:* pilot group. *Done when:* each use case has one agreed prompt,
saved somewhere everyone can reach, with the placeholders written out.

**Week 8 — the honest read.**
Compare the log against the baseline. Ask three questions and answer them
in writing:

1. Did the task get faster once review time is included? Review time
   counts. A draft produced in two minutes that takes forty minutes to
   check has not saved you thirty-eight minutes.
2. Did rework go up, down, or stay flat?
3. Would the reviewer be comfortable if this output went out under their
   name every month?

If the answers are good, you widen. If they are mixed, you extend the
pilot for a month rather than widening — an extension is a legitimate
decision and it will make the eventual answer stronger. If they are poor,
you stop that use case and say why, in one paragraph, to the whole team.

*Who:* owner writes, sponsor reads. *Done when:* a one-page written
finding exists, with the log attached.

**How phase two most commonly fails.** The pilot group logs the successes
and forgets the failures, usually without meaning to. People remember the
run that worked and skip logging the three that did not, and by week 8 the
data says the pilot went beautifully while the reviewer is quietly
rewriting everything. Two defences: ask for the worst output, not the
best, every week; and treat the reviewer's correction time as the real
measure, because it is the one number nobody can flatter.

The other failure is the reviewer being cut out. Once people find the
output "usually fine", the review step starts getting skipped under
deadline pressure, and the first time you learn about it is when something
wrong has left the building. Make sign-off a recorded step, not a habit.

### Phase three — Days 61 to 90: widen only what held

**The goal.** Move from a pilot that worked to a routine the team follows
without you standing over it, and leave behind something that survives the
owner going on leave.

**Week 9 — write the run sheets.**
For each surviving use case, write a one-page run sheet: the exact prompt
with placeholders, what to attach, what to check before accepting the
output, who signs off, and where the result is saved. If it does not fit
on one page, the workflow is too complicated to hand over and you should
simplify it before you spread it.

*Who:* pilot group writes, owner edits. *Done when:* one page per use
case, in the same place as the policy.

**Week 10 — teach the next group.**
The pilot group teaches Levels 1 and 2 to the next cohort, with the owner
present. The people who did it teaching the people who have not is more
convincing than any external session, and it exposes gaps in your run
sheets within about twenty minutes.

*Who:* pilot group teaches. *Done when:* the second cohort has run the
workflow once each, under supervision.

**Week 11 — a deliberate stress test.**
Run one period-end, or one client job, with the new workflow in place and
the owner not intervening. Log it. The interesting output is the list of
questions people asked that the run sheet did not answer.

*Who:* the new cohort. *Done when:* the run sheet has been amended with
the answers to those questions.

**Week 12 — review the policy against reality.**
You now know things you did not know on day 14. Update the policy: the
approved tools list, the data rules that turned out to be unworkable or
too loose, the sign-off record, the failure types you found. Get the
sponsor to re-approve. Re-circulate. Two-page limit still applies.

*Who:* owner and data/IT contact. *Done when:* version two is signed and
sent.

**Week 13 — decide what happens next, and write it down.**
One page to the sponsor: what you tried, what the log says, what you have
stopped doing, what the next two use cases are, and what you are
deliberately not doing yet. Add the standing arrangement: who keeps the
log, how often it is reviewed, and when the policy is next looked at.

*Who:* owner. *Done when:* the sponsor has the page and the next review
date is in a calendar.

**How phase three most commonly fails.** Everything widens at once. The
pilot held for two use cases with five people who had been trained and
watched; it is then treated as a general permission, thirty people start
using it for whatever they like, quality drops, and the whole thing gets
banned in month five by someone reacting to a single bad incident. Widen
the use cases you tested, with the training you tested, and leave the rest
on the list.

The quieter failure is that nothing sticks because the owner was the only
one who ever cared. If, by week 13, no one other than the owner can run
the workflow from the run sheet, you have a hobby rather than a process.

### The senior who will not engage

You will have one. Often more than one, and often your best technical
reviewer, which is not a coincidence — they got good by not trusting
things.

Do not put them in the pilot group. Do not sit them in a demonstration.
Both read as pressure and produce a public position they then have to
defend for a year.

Instead, give them the role they are already good at: reviewer. Ask them
to be the person who checks the pilot output and tells you what is wrong
with it. That is an honest job, it uses their scepticism as an asset, and
it puts them in contact with the actual quality of the output rather than
the claims about it. Several people who start out flatly opposed end up
adopting parts of it in their own work once they have seen where it fails,
because now they know the shape of the risk. Some do not, which is a
legitimate outcome as long as they are not blocking the team.

Two things to hold firm on. They do not get to veto other people's use
inside the policy. And they do get to say "not on my client work" for a
period, if they carry the professional responsibility for it — that is not
obstruction, it is someone exercising judgement they are accountable for.
If your work is regulated, whose name is on the file matters more than
your adoption plan does.

What does not work: making it a performance objective, mocking them in
front of juniors, or going around them to their staff. All three convert a
sceptic into an opponent, and opponents are much more expensive.

### The junior who has already raced ahead

You will have one of these too, usually a competent qualified-recently type
who has been using an assistant for six months, is genuinely faster at
some things, and has been quietly building their own way of working with
it.

Your instinct will be to slow them down. Half-resist it. What you need
from them, immediately and explicitly, is honesty about what they have
already put into which tool — you cannot manage exposure you do not know
about. Ask directly, once, with the same no-consequences framing as week 1.

Then give them a real job: writing prompts and run sheets for the pilot,
and teaching Level 2. This turns private practice into a documented team
asset and it gives them status for doing the thing they were going to do
anyway, which is far more effective than a warning.

The one line you hold is review. The specific risk with a fast, confident
junior is not that they use the tool; it is that they produce more work
than their reviewer's normal capacity, at a quality that looks finished.
Polished, well-formatted output invites a lighter read. Say this to the
reviewer out loud: the drafts now look better than they used to, and the
appearance of the work no longer tells you much about the care behind it.
Check the numbers and the source references, not the prose.

If they have been using an unapproved tool on client data, deal with it as
an exposure to be assessed and reported per your own obligations, not as a
character question. Whether it needs to be reported anywhere is a matter
for your professional body's rules and your local law, and you should ask
rather than assume.

### The ninety days on one page

| Week | Phase | What happens | Who leads | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Contain and choose | Ask everyone what they already use; issue the one rule | Owner | Written list of current use; one rule circulated |
| 2 | | Draft the two-page policy; check tool terms and data obligations | Owner + data/IT | Sponsor signs; team confirms they have read it |
| 3 | | Choose exactly two use cases against the four tests | Owner + pilot group | Two one-sentence use cases with named reviewers |
| 4 | | Record the "before": time and rework, labelled as estimates | Pilot group | Three baseline observations per use case |
| 5 | Pilot | Levels 1–2 training; pilot begins; every run logged | Owner | Two logged runs per person |
| 6 | | "Show me the worst output" review; list failure types | Owner + reviewer | Written failure list circulated |
| 7 | | Level 3 training; tighten prompts; drop what is not working | Pilot group | One agreed saved prompt per use case |
| 8 | | Compare against baseline; decide widen, extend or stop | Owner + sponsor | One-page written finding with log attached |
| 9 | Widen what held | Write one-page run sheets per use case | Pilot group | One page each, stored with the policy |
| 10 | | Pilot group teaches Levels 1–2 to the next cohort | Pilot group | Second cohort has run it once, supervised |
| 11 | | Stress test on a real period-end or job, owner hands off | New cohort | Run sheet amended with the gaps found |
| 12 | | Update policy against what actually happened | Owner + data/IT | Version two signed and re-circulated |
| 13 | | Write up; set the standing review; name the next two use cases | Owner | Sponsor has the page; next review date booked |

## Part two: a four-level training curriculum

This is designed to be taught by a manager who is one step ahead of the
room, not by a specialist. Each level stands alone. Nobody needs Level 4
unless they are designing workflows, and most of your team will get most
of the benefit from Levels 1 to 3.

What you need to run it: a room with a screen, a working licence for
whatever tool you have approved, and real examples from your own work with
client-identifiable details removed. Made-up examples do not land with this
audience; they will spot that the numbers are not real and switch off.

Teach in the order given. The most common curriculum mistake is starting
at Level 2 because prompting seems like the practical bit. Without Level 1,
people write better prompts and trust the answers more, which is the worst
combination available.

| Level | For | Length | The point |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Everyone | 45 minutes, one session | What it is and why it is confident when wrong |
| 2 | Everyone who will use it | 90 minutes, two sessions | Writing a prompt that produces usable work |
| 3 | Anyone whose output is reviewed or reviews others | 2 × 60 minutes | Verification, and working with your own documents |
| 4 | Managers and process owners | 3 × 60 minutes plus follow-up | Repeatable workflows, and when to stop |

### Level 1 — What the thing actually is, and why it is confident when wrong

**Who it is for.** Everyone in the finance function, including the people
who will never use it. Especially the people who review other people's
work.

**Length.** Forty-five minutes. One session. Do not extend it; the content
is small and the demonstration does the work.

**Learning outcomes.** By the end, each person can say in their own words:
that the tool predicts plausible text rather than looking up facts; that
fluency is not evidence of accuracy; that it will invent a reference,
a figure or a paragraph number with exactly the same confident tone it
uses when it is right; that it does not know what it does not know; and
that its confident tone is a property of how it writes, not a signal about
how sure it is.

**Session outline.**

1. *Ten minutes — what it is doing.* One explanation, no jargon: it
   produces the next piece of text that fits, based on patterns in an
   enormous amount of writing. It is very good at the shape of a document
   — a memo reads like a memo, a reconciliation note reads like a
   reconciliation note. The shape being right tells you nothing about
   whether the contents are.
2. *Fifteen minutes — the live exercise below.* This is the session.
3. *Ten minutes — where it is strong.* Rewriting, summarising a document
   you provide, drafting a first version, explaining something in simpler
   words, spotting what is missing from a list. Note what these have in
   common: you supply the substance, it supplies the form.
4. *Five minutes — where it is weak.* Anything requiring it to know a fact
   you did not give it. Arithmetic you have not checked. Anything current.
   Anything where being 95% right is the same as being wrong.
5. *Five minutes — the team's rule.* Read out the one rule about named
   human review, and the data rules from your policy.

**The live exercise: the confident wrong answer.**
On screen, in front of everyone, run these two prompts in order. Do not
rehearse them first — the point is that you do not know what it will say
either.

```
Summarise the disclosure requirements for [TOPIC] under [ACCOUNTING FRAMEWORK]
for an entity of type [ENTITY TYPE]. Quote the exact paragraph reference for
each requirement and state which pronouncement it comes from.
```

Then, whatever it produces, put the reference into your actual source
material and read out what is really there. Sometimes it will be right.
Sometimes it will produce a reference in the correct format that does not
exist, or attach a real reference to the wrong requirement. Either result
teaches the lesson, because the tone is identical both times.

Then run:

```
Here is a trial balance extract. Calculate the movement in each account
between [PERIOD 1] and [PERIOD 2], the percentage change, and tell me which
three movements a reviewer should question first.

[PASTE 15-20 ROWS OF A REAL TRIAL BALANCE, ANONYMISED]
```

Have someone check every arithmetic line on a calculator while the room
watches. Discuss what happened. If it got the arithmetic right, that is
also a useful result — say plainly that one correct run is not a
guarantee, and that this is why the checking step is not optional.

**How you tell whether it landed.** At the end, ask each person to write
one sentence: *why did it produce a confident wrong answer?* Collect the
slips. If most of them say something about the data being out of date, it
did not land — that is the "it needs newer information" model, and it
leads people to trust it on anything historic. Re-run the exercise with a
different topic. What you want to see is people describing it producing
text that fits rather than text that is true.

The real test comes a fortnight later. Listen for the question people ask
about someone else's draft. "Is this right?" means Level 1 did not land.
"What did you check this against?" means it did.

### Level 2 — Writing a usable prompt

**Who it is for.** Everyone who will actually use the tool for work.

**Length.** Ninety minutes, split into two forty-five minute sessions a
week apart, with homework in between. The gap matters; people need to try
it badly once on their own before the second half is useful.

**Learning outcomes.** Each person can write a prompt that states the
role, the context, the task, the constraints and the output format; can
supply source material rather than expecting the tool to know things; can
ask it to show its working or flag its assumptions; and can recognise when
a bad output is caused by a bad prompt rather than by a bad tool.

**Session outline.**

*Session A (45 minutes).*
1. *Five minutes — the failure they have all seen.* Someone types "write
   a variance analysis", gets something generic, concludes it is useless.
2. *Fifteen minutes — the five parts.* Role, context, task, constraints,
   format. Walk through each with a finance example. The part finance
   people skip is context: the entity, the framework, the period, the
   materiality, who reads the output.
3. *Twenty minutes — the live exercise below.*
4. *Five minutes — homework.* Everyone brings one real task and the prompt
   they wrote for it, plus the output, good or bad.

*Session B (45 minutes).*
1. *Twenty-five minutes — workshop the homework.* Put prompts on screen
   anonymously. Fix them as a group. This is the most valuable half hour
   in the whole curriculum.
2. *Ten minutes — iteration.* Show that the second and third messages in a
   conversation do more than the first: "that is too long", "drop the
   introduction", "you have assumed [X], I meant [Y]".
3. *Ten minutes — build the shared prompt list.* Every prompt that worked
   goes in one place, with placeholders, so nobody rewrites it next month.

**The live exercise: two prompts, one task.**
Run the thin version first:

```
Write a variance analysis commentary.
```

Read the result out. It will be plausible and useless. Then run:

```
You are drafting internal management commentary for the finance team of
[ENTITY], a [INDUSTRY] business reporting under [ACCOUNTING FRAMEWORK], for
the period [PERIOD]. The audience is [AUDIENCE], who are not accountants.

Below is the actual variance data. Using only the figures given:
1. Write one paragraph per variance above [THRESHOLD].
2. For each, state the movement in both absolute and percentage terms.
3. Where the data does not explain a cause, say that the cause is not
   determinable from the data provided. Do not speculate about causes.
4. List separately any figure you could not reconcile.

Constraints: maximum [NUMBER] words. Plain English. No adjectives about
performance. Do not describe any result as strong, weak, disappointing or
encouraging.

Data:
[PASTE VARIANCE TABLE]
```

Compare the two on screen. Point out specifically what the instruction "do
not speculate about causes" prevented — invented explanations for variances
are one of the most common and most damaging failure modes in finance
drafting, because they read exactly like knowledge.

**How you tell whether it landed.** Two weeks after session B, look at the
shared prompt list. If it has entries from more than half the attendees,
it landed. If it has three entries, all from the owner, it did not — and
the usual reason is that people are still using it in a private chat window
for things they do not consider "real work". Ask them what they used it for
yesterday; the answer is usually more informative than the list.

### Level 3 — Verification, and working with your team's own documents

**Who it is for.** Anyone whose output gets reviewed, and everyone who
reviews. In practice this is most of the team.

**Length.** Two sessions of sixty minutes, ideally a week apart.

**Learning outcomes.** Each person can name what must be checked in a given
output and check it efficiently rather than re-doing the work; can ground a
request in supplied documents and require the tool to quote its source
lines; can recognise the specific failure of a confident summary of a
document that says something slightly different; and can decide when
verification costs more than the assistance saved, and say so.

**Session outline.**

*Session A — verification.*
1. *Ten minutes — the reviewer's problem.* Output now arrives looking
   finished. The old signals — clumsy phrasing, inconsistent formatting —
   no longer tell you how much care went in.
2. *Fifteen minutes — the four checks.* Numbers: recalculate, do not read.
   Sources: does the quoted line exist in the document, in those words?
   Omissions: what is missing, which no output will tell you. Claims: any
   sentence asserting a fact you did not supply is unverified until you
   verify it.
3. *Twenty-five minutes — the live exercise below.*
4. *Ten minutes — recording it.* How your team evidences that a review
   happened. Whatever your file or working paper conventions are, decide
   this now rather than inventing it per job.

*Session B — your own documents.*
1. *Fifteen minutes — grounding.* The difference between asking it about a
   policy and giving it the policy. Give it the document, every time.
2. *Twenty minutes — the quoting technique.* Requiring the tool to quote
   the exact line it relied on, so that verification takes seconds rather
   than a re-read.
3. *Fifteen minutes — the limits.* Long documents get summarised
   unevenly, and the middle is where things go missing. Split them. Ask
   about one section at a time.
4. *Ten minutes — the data rules again.* Which of your documents may be
   uploaded at all, under your policy and your obligations. This will be
   the most-asked question in the whole curriculum, so have the answer
   written down.

**The live exercise: find the three planted errors.**
Before the session, take a real piece of assisted output — a summary of an
internal policy, or a commentary on a set of figures — and plant exactly
three errors: one arithmetic, one a quoted phrase that does not appear in
the source, and one material omission. Do not tell the room how many
errors there are, or that they were planted, until afterwards.

Give everyone the output and the source documents. Fifteen minutes,
working in pairs. Then compare what each pair found.

Almost every group finds the arithmetic error and misses the omission. That
is the lesson, and it is much better felt than told: what is missing does
not announce itself, and no amount of reading the output will reveal it.
Only knowing what should have been there does.

Then teach the fix. Run this prompt on the same source material:

```
Using only the document below, answer this question: [QUESTION].

For every statement you make, quote the exact sentence from the document
that supports it, in quotation marks, immediately after the statement.
If the document does not address part of my question, list those parts
under a heading "Not covered by this document". Do not use any knowledge
from outside the document.

Document:
[PASTE DOCUMENT]
```

Show that the "Not covered" list is the part worth reading first. Check two
of the quotes against the source in front of the room, including one that
turns out to be paraphrased rather than quoted — if you cannot produce one
naturally, do not fake it; say that paraphrase-instead-of-quote is a
failure to watch for and move on.

**How you tell whether it landed.** Look at the pilot log. If the "rework
needed?" column starts getting more entries after Level 3, the training
worked — people are now catching things they previously accepted. A pilot
whose error rate appears to fall immediately after verification training is
usually a pilot that has stopped looking properly. Tell the team that in
advance, so that finding errors reads as doing the job well rather than as
a bad week.

### Level 4 — Designing a repeatable workflow, and knowing when to stop

**Who it is for.** Managers, process owners, and the one or two people who
will maintain this after the ninety days.

**Length.** Three sessions of sixty minutes, plus a follow-up four weeks
later to review what was built.

**Learning outcomes.** Each person can convert an ad hoc use into a
documented workflow with a fixed prompt, defined inputs, a checking step
and a named sign-off; can estimate whether the workflow is actually worth
it once review time is counted; can recognise a task that should not be
automated at all; and can retire a workflow that has stopped earning its
place.

**Session outline.**

*Session A — from ad hoc to repeatable.* What makes a task suitable:
frequency, stable inputs, an existing check, a tolerable failure mode. The
anatomy of a run sheet: trigger, inputs, prompt with placeholders,
processing steps, checks, sign-off, where the output is stored. Each
attendee picks one candidate from their own work.

*Session B — build one.* Attendees write their run sheet in the room and
swap with a neighbour, who must try to follow it exactly as written and
mark every point where they had to guess. A run sheet somebody else cannot
follow is not finished.

*Session C — knowing when to stop.* Four stop signals, in order of how
often they apply:

1. Verification costs more than the drafting saved. Count the review
   minutes honestly. If they exceed the time saved, stop; the workflow is
   moving effort, not reducing it.
2. The failure mode is intolerable regardless of frequency. If a wrong
   output goes straight out with no human between it and the reader, the
   error rate does not need to be high to be unacceptable.
3. The task is the training. Some tasks are how juniors learn the
   business. Automating the first draft of a reconciliation note may cost
   you something you will not notice for two years. This is a judgement
   call, and it is yours to make deliberately rather than by default.
4. Nobody can explain the output. If the person signing cannot say how the
   result was arrived at, they are signing something they do not
   understand, and their name is still on it.

*Follow-up session, four weeks later.* Each attendee reports on their
workflow using the log. Retire at least one thing. A curriculum that never
retires anything is accumulating obligations.

**The live exercise: build and run the month-end commentary workflow.**
Do this as a group, on the real task, in the session. Write the run sheet
on screen. Then run it end to end with real anonymised data while somebody
times each step and writes the numbers where everyone can see them.
Include the review time. Then ask the room the only question that matters:
knowing these numbers, would you do this next month?

Sometimes the answer is no. Let it be no. A Level 4 session that ends in a
documented decision not to automate something is a success, and it will do
more for your credibility with the sceptics than three that end in
enthusiasm.

Use this prompt as the workflow's fixed step, filled in and saved:

```
You are producing the [PERIOD] management commentary for [ENTITY], following
the same structure as the attached previous version.

Inputs: the current period figures below, and last period's commentary for
structure and tone only — do not carry forward any figure or explanation
from it.

Produce:
1. A commentary section for each of [SECTIONS], in the same order as the
   previous version.
2. Movements stated in both absolute and percentage terms.
3. A separate list headed "Requires input from the business" for anything
   the figures alone do not explain.
4. A separate list headed "Checks for the reviewer" naming every figure you
   calculated rather than copied.

Do not state causes that are not evidenced in the data provided. Do not
characterise performance.

Current period figures:
[PASTE]

Previous commentary:
[PASTE]
```

The fourth instruction is the one that earns its place: a list of what the
tool calculated tells the reviewer exactly where to point a calculator.

**How you tell whether it landed.** Four weeks later, look for two things:
at least one workflow running without the trainer, and at least one
workflow retired or never started because the numbers did not support it.
If everything survives, nobody applied the stop signals, and you have
taught enthusiasm rather than judgement.

## When it stalls — and it usually does

Adoption commonly stalls somewhere between weeks six and ten. The novelty
has worn off, month-end has arrived, and the people who were logging
diligently have gone quiet. This is normal enough that you should plan for
it rather than treat it as a verdict.

A stall is information. Read what it is telling you before you react,
because the cure differs entirely by cause:

- **It stalled at month-end.** Nothing is wrong. People fell back to the
  known method under deadline pressure, which is a reasonable thing for a
  professional to do. Restart the following week and expect the same thing
  next month until the workflow is genuinely faster than the old one under
  pressure, not just in a quiet week.
- **It stalled because the output was not good enough.** The most useful
  outcome available to you. Something you hoped would work does not, on
  your data, for your task. Write that down specifically — not "it isn't
  accurate" but "it could not reconcile the intercompany balances without
  more instruction than the task saved". That sentence is worth more than
  a successful pilot on a task you did not care about.
- **It stalled because verification cost too much.** Legitimate. Either
  narrow the task so the check is cheaper, or stop. Do not solve it by
  checking less.
- **It stalled because one person was carrying it.** The most common cause
  and the least discussed. The owner got busy, and nothing had been
  handed over. Fix the handover, not the enthusiasm.
- **It stalled because nobody was ever asked to.** Also common. There was a
  policy and a licence and no instruction. If you want a task done a
  particular way, ask for it in the way you ask for anything else.

What not to do: relaunch. A second launch with more energy and a new name,
aimed at the same people who watched the first one fade, costs you
credibility you will want later. Fix the specific cause, quietly, and let
the second attempt be smaller than the first.

What to do instead is dull and works. Return to one use case, with one
group, with the log. Ask the reviewer what they are still correcting. Put
the next review date in the calendar and keep it even when there is nothing
to report — especially then, because "nothing happened this month" is the
finding that most often needs saying out loud.

And be willing to conclude that some of it does not suit your team, your
work or your obligations right now. That is a defensible professional
judgement, it is a great deal cheaper than a slow expensive drift, and it
leaves you free to look again in six months with a log full of things you
actually know rather than things you were told.
